title: How the Cannonball Run Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Cannonball Run, the illegal cross-country race started by automotive journalist Brock Yates in 1971 after he became concerned about the national 55 mph speed limit. They cover Yates's first solo run from New York to Los Angeles, the Polish Racing Drivers of America telegram, the namesake Cannonball Baker and his motorcycle exploits, the rules and the 1971 race won by Yates and Dan Gurney in a Ferrari Daytona, later races and corporate sponsorship, the 1979 final race that inspired the movie Cannonball Run with Burt Reynolds, imitators like Gumball Rally and the European Cannonball Run, and hosts' personal speeding stories. The episode also includes a listener mail from Ryan Hack and a Kiva plug.
topics: Cannonball Baker Sea to Shining Sea Memorial Trophy Dash

segments.title: Opening banter and 1979 setup
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter and set the scene with 1979 news, then introduce Burt Reynolds' movie Cannonball Run, which was originally meant to be serious and based on a real race.

segments.title: Brock Yates and the 55 mph speed limit
segments.summary: Brock Yates is described as a premier automotive journalist. The hosts contrast his pro-speed view with Ralph Nader's safety campaign that led to seatbelts and safety rules, then explain the 55 mph national speed limit as a response to the Arab oil embargo.

segments.title: Yates's 1971 New York to Los Angeles drive
segments.summary: In 1971 Yates drove a Dodge Van from New York to Los Angeles in 40 hours 51 minutes as a protest that good drivers and cars could drive fast safely. A telegram from the Polish Racing Drivers of America then formally entered the next race.
topics: Cannonball Baker Sea to Shining Sea Memorial Trophy Dash

segments.title: Cannonball Baker and the race name
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the race honors Cannonball Baker, a motorcycle endurance rider known for cross-country rides, and that the name was shortened from Cannon Ball Baker to Cannonball to avoid legal issues.

segments.title: First official race rules and 1971 winners
segments.summary: The first official race had several entrants, including a Cadillac driven for a New York owner. Rules were loose: any route, twenty-four hour window, time clock punches, fifty-dollar entry fee. Yates and Dan Gurney won in a Ferrari Daytona in 35 hours 54 minutes. Tactics included going slow in the East and fast on the Great Plains.

segments.title: Later races, sponsorship, and the 1979 race
segments.summary: The second race drew 25 entries and Yates finished second in a Cadillac. A 1975 race had corporate sponsorship. Yates ended the race series, then Hal Needham staged a final race in 1979 with a record 46 entries, which inspired the movie. Real events included an ambulance entry and priest-disguised drivers.

segments.title: Movie details and imitators
segments.summary: The hosts compare real events from the final race with the movie and mention imitators, including Cannonball! and the Gumball Rally, and the European Cannonball Run, which is a non-race road trip averaging about 61 mph.

segments.title: Hosts' personal speeding stories
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh share personal speeding stories, including Chuck being pulled over at 110 mph and a friend's drive to see a Star Wars prequel at speed in Vermont.

segments.title: Listener mail and Kiva plug
segments.summary: A listener named Ryan Hack shares a creepy house story and is thanked, then the hosts promote a Kiva team and ask for listener fast stories.
